title: China proposes export controls on its advanced AI models and chip designs
content:
China’s commerce and science ministries proposed adding 23 AI technologies, including large models, agents, chip designs, and computing clusters, to the country’s export control list. Open-source tech is exempt and overseas users can still access models through apps. A temporary export registration rule took effect on 16 October.
China plans to limit exports of 23 AI technologies, from large language models and AI agents to chip designs. Its commerce and science ministries put out the draft proposal on Friday.
The plan covers 40 items in total. Besides AI, it lists 12 solar items and five in biomedicine, such as gene therapy. The public can comment until 15 November.
For large models, the curbs would cover weights, source code, and other core parts. They would apply to models with at least 2 trillion parameters, or that rank in the world’s top 10 on tests such as performance and safety, Bloomberg reported.
Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max are among the models above that size, according to Bloomberg and the Associated Press. The draft itself does not name any model.
The draft would also limit design know-how for AI chips made at 14 nanometres or below, or built by stacking chips in 2.5D or 3D. Some memory chip designs are on the list too.
However, open-source code and published research would be exempt. Chinese firms could also keep serving users abroad through apps, websites, and APIs, the ministry said.
Running a covered model on servers abroad would count as an export. Still, firms that run it on their own cloud servers abroad could get a licence automatically.
The rules aim to “prevent misuse and abuse” and “ensure that AI remains under human control,” a ministry spokesperson said in a statement.
The ministry added that the plan does not target any country or firm. Meanwhile, firms must now register before they export any of the listed items, under a temporary rule that took effect on Friday. It also covers deals that are not yet complete.
Earlier this year, Beijing was reported to be weighing limits on overseas access to its top models. In July, the Financial Times reported that it was considering export controls on AI models and chips.

report.summary: China proposed export controls on 23 advanced AI technologies, including large-model weights and chip designs, while exempting open-source code and offshore app access.
report.background: China’s proposal comes as AI model capability and chip design are increasingly treated as strategic assets. The U.S. has restricted advanced chip exports to China, and Beijing has been building its own AI stack and legal toolkit. Chinese open-weight models such as Qwen and Kimi have gained global developer traction, raising questions about whether weights, source code, and chip design know-how should be controlled. The draft is broader than AI: it covers 40 items in AI, solar, and biomedicine, and follows a temporary export registration rule. It also reflects a balancing act: officials want to prevent misuse and retain human control, but avoid cutting off overseas app/API users or open-source collaboration. The public comment period and earlier reports that Beijing was weighing model controls suggest this is a deliberate policy signal, not a finalized ban.
key_points: The draft adds 23 AI technologies—large models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters—to export controls, within a 40-item package that also covers solar and biomedicine. For models, controls would touch weights, source code and core components when a model has at least 2 trillion parameters or ranks in the global top 10 on performance or safety tests.

Open-source code and published research would be exempt, and Chinese firms could continue serving overseas users through apps, websites and APIs. However, running a covered model on servers abroad would count as an export; firms using their own overseas cloud servers could receive an automatic licence, softening the rules for some deployments.

The proposal would restrict design know-how for AI chips made at 14 nanometres or below, or built using 2.5D or 3D stacking. Some memory chip designs are also listed. That extends scrutiny beyond model weights into the semiconductor design layer, where advanced packaging and process nodes are central to AI compute.

A temporary export registration rule took effect on 16 October, requiring firms to register before exporting listed items, including deals not yet completed. The draft is open for public comment until 15 November. Officials say the aim is to prevent misuse and keep AI under human control, not to target any country or company.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the draft signals that model weights, source code and chip design know-how are becoming export-controlled strategic goods, mirroring U.S. semiconductor restrictions. Chinese labs may formalize licensing and offshore cloud strategies; global firms may need provenance and compliance checks when using Chinese models. Developers could see more friction around high-end model access and chip design collaboration, but open-source exemptions and app/API carve-outs limit immediate disruption. Regular users may still access Chinese AI apps abroad, though future premium or largest models could be gated. The bigger effect is uncertainty: open-weight releases may accelerate as a safe channel, while closed frontier models face compliance costs.
report.tools: To follow the policy, watch MOFCOM and MOST export-control catalogues; track open-weight releases on Hugging Face and ModelScope (Qwen, Kimi); use license/provenance scanners such as ScanCode and FOSSA; screen parties against BIS Consolidated Screening List and EU dual-use lists; and map governance with NIST AI RMF. These help developers assess model access, licensing and compliance risk as the draft evolves.
